chunk_findings.detail: `anchors_of` stores explicit HTML anchors verbatim — `out.update(_HTML_ANCHOR.findall(line))` keeps the attribute value exactly as written — but `_link` compares `if frag.lower() not in offered`. For a document containing `` (or `id="MyAnchor"`) and the canonical, exactly-matching link `[x](#MyAnchor)`, `frag.lower()` is `"myanchor"`, `offered` is `{"MyAnchor"}`, so the check emits `Finding("anchor", ..., "no heading #MyAnchor in ")`. Every explicit anchor whose id contains an uppercase letter is reported as broken, even when the link is correct. (Conversely, a wrong-case link to a `name`/`id` is silently accepted, since the low end of the comparison was normalized and the other was not.) The comparison has to be normalized on both sides, or on neither.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck.py: `_Scan._link` (anchor comparison) vs `anchors_of` (`_HTML_ANCHOR`)

chunk_findings.detail:
Only ATX headings are recognized (`_ATX` requires `#{1,6}` plus whitespace). Setext headings (`Title` followed by `=====` / `-----`) render as headings on GitHub and get slugs, but produce no entry in `offered`. Given

```
Title
=====

See [the intro](#title).
```

`anchors_of` returns an empty/other set and `_link` reports `no heading #title in doc.md`, although `#title` is exactly the anchor GitHub serves for that document.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck.py: `anchors_of` / `slugify`

chunk_findings.detail:
The fence state machine keys only on the first character of the run — `fence = None if fence == mark else (fence or mark)` — and never tracks the run length, so a shorter fence line inside a longer one closes it. Input:

````
# T

````
```
run `missing_ident_xyz`
```
````
````

Per CommonMark the ```` fence is only closed by four backticks, so lines 4–6 are code. Here line 4 ("```") sets `fence = None`, so line 5 is treated as prose and `_span` runs the identifier check on `missing_ident_xyz`, emitting an `identifier` finding for a name that lives inside a code block. (With an odd number of backtick-prefixed lines in such a block the state ends up open, after which the rest of the document is scanned as code, suppressing link/anchor checks and running `_command` over prose.)
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck.py: `_Scan.run` and `anchors_of` fence toggling

chunk_findings.detail: This test wraps `D.check_docs(root, docs=["README.md"])` in a wall-clock bound (`assert time.perf_counter() - start < 2.0`). `check_docs` shells out to git and parses every tracked non-doc file in the tree, so the measured time is dominated by machine state (cold page cache, loaded/oversubscribed CI runner, large checkout), not by the checker's behavior. On such a runner the identical, correct implementation exceeds 2 s and the suite fails spuriously, which is a failure mode that cannot be fixed from the code under test. The same test also hard-codes `report.checked["identifiers"] > 100`, pinning the assertion to the current README's inline-code volume: any later README edit that drops inline code below that count breaks the test even though `docscheck` is unchanged (and keeping README in sync with code is exactly what this tool exists to encourage).
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_docscheck_core.py:test_runtime_on_this_repositorys_readme

chunk_findings.detail:
`_REFDEF` accepts any line of the shape `[label]: <first-token> …` as a link reference definition and feeds `group(1)` to `_link()`. GitHub footnote definitions and definition-list lines have exactly that shape, but they are not links. Input: a document containing

```
[^1]: See the [install](docs/install.md) page.
```

`_REFDEF.match` returns `group(1) == "See"`; `_link("See")` finds no `See` in the tree and appends `Finding("link", <doc>, <n>, "See", "See is not in the tree")`. A perfectly valid document therefore produces a finding (and a non-clean report). The destination should be required to look like a link/URL/path (scheme, `/`, or a file-ish token), not just any non-space token — a footnote's prose is arbitrary.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck.py — `_Scan.run` / `_REFDEF`

chunk_findings.detail:
Setext heading text is only accumulated into `paragraph` when the line does not start with `-`, `*`, `+`, `>`, or `|`:

```python
elif line.strip() and not line.lstrip().startswith(("-", "*", "+", ">", "|")):
    paragraph.append(line.strip())
```

That test is meant to exclude list items, but it also excludes ordinary paragraph lines that begin with emphasis. Input:

```
**Install**
===

Run [the installer](#install).
```

On GitHub `**Install**` + `===` is a valid setext h2 whose slug is `install`. Here line 1 begins with `*`, so `paragraph` stays empty; line 2 (`===`, which does not begin with an excluded character) is instead appended as paragraph text, and no `install` anchor is registered. The link `#install` on line 4 then yields `Finding("anchor", …, "no heading #install in <doc>")` — a false positive on a document whose anchor resolves fine on GitHub. The same mis-accumulation of the underline line (`===`) can additionally fabricate an unrelated anchor when a later `---` line follows.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck.py — `anchors_of`

chunk_findings.detail: `_REFDEF` is `^\s{0,3}\[[^\]]+\]:\s*<?(\S+?)>?...`, i.e. it matches *any* line beginning with `[label]:`, not only link-reference definitions. GitHub footnote definitions have exactly that shape. For a document containing `[^1]: See the appendix.`, `run()` calls `self._link("See", n)`; `_link` sees no scheme, no `//`, no `{`/`<`, so it counts a link, resolves `docs/See` (or `See`), finds it is not in the tree, and appends `Finding("link", ..., "See is not in the tree")`. The checker therefore reports a broken relative link for a line that is not a link at all, and any doc using GitHub footnotes produces a permanent, unfixable finding (`Report.clean` is False). The regex needs at least to exclude the `[^...]` footnote-label form before treating the target as a URL.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck.py:_REFDEF (used by `_Scan.run`)

chunk_findings.detail: The doc-side flag pattern `_FLAG` accepts a two-character long flag (`--[a-z][a-z0-9]*…` matches `--x`), but the corpus pattern requires at least two characters after `--` (`--[a-z][a-z0-9-]*[a-z0-9]`). So for code that spells `--x` — e.g. `parser.add_argument("--x")` — `_Corpus.build` can never put `--x` into `corpus.flags` (the lookahead to `[a-z0-9]` fails on the closing quote), and a document that writes `` `--x` `` is always reported with `flag ... no tracked code spells this flag`, regardless of the code. The two patterns should agree on the minimum flag length (or `_FLAG` should reject single-letter long flags).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck.py:_CORPUS_FLAG

chunk_findings.detail: The document-side flag pattern `_FLAG = --[a-z][a-z0-9]*(?:-[a-z0-9]+)*` accepts a one-letter long flag, but the corpus-side pattern `_CORPUS_FLAG = (?<![\w-])--[a-z][a-z0-9-]*[a-z0-9]` requires at least two characters after `--`, so a one-letter flag can never be present in `corpus.flags`. Given a tracked file containing `parser.add_argument("--x")` and a document line ``Pass `--x` to disable.``, `_span` extracts `--x`, `_FLAG.fullmatch` succeeds, and `_flag` emits `Finding("flag", ..., "--x", "no tracked code spells this flag")` even though the code spells exactly that flag. The two regexes must accept the same token shape or the check is unsatisfiable for that shape.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck.py: `_CORPUS_FLAG` vs `_FLAG`

chunk_findings.detail: The destination capture `[^)\s>]+` stops at the first `)`, so a CommonMark-valid destination with a balanced parenthesis pair is truncated. Given a tracked file `docs/a_(b).md` and a document line `[spec](docs/a_(b).md)`, `_LINK` captures `docs/a_(b`, `_link` resolves it (via `posixpath.join(self.dir, ...)`) to `docs/a_(b`, `_Tree.has` is false, and a `link` finding is emitted whose `ref`/`detail` name a path that does not exist — while CommonMark and GitHub resolve the link to `docs/a_(b).md`, which is in the tree. `_path`'s `_PATHY` handles `_(b).md` fine, but the link rule cannot, so the two halves of the check disagree on the same filename.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck.py: `_LINK`

chunk_findings.detail: `unquote(url)` is applied to the whole URL *before* `.partition("#")` and `target.partition("?")`, so percent-encoded `#`/`?` inside a filename are reinterpreted as the fragment/query delimiter. Given a tracked file `a#b.md` and the correct, encoded link `[x](a%23b.md)`, `unquote` yields `a#b.md`, `partition("#")` gives `target="a"`, `frag="b.md"`, and since `tree.has("a")` is false the report gets `Finding("link", ..., "a%23b.md", "a is not in the tree")`. The same happens for a file named `a?b.md` linked as `a%3Fb.md` (target becomes empty and the fragment is silently treated as an anchor). Splitting on the delimiters first and unquoting the pieces afterwards gives the right target.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck.py: `_Scan._link`

chunk_findings.detail: The test asserts that the OLD_README yields exactly three drifts, but that fixture also contains the inline-code command `ddflow lesson add` (in the table row for “record a lesson / decision / research / bug”). The provided `CODE` fixture registers only first-level subcommands `loops`, `workflow`, `lesson`, `decision`, `research`, `bug` (no nested `add` subparser) and the `TOOLS` list has `ddflow_lesson_add` only as a separate tool name. A command check matching the stated intent (“inline-code … commands that name nothing in tracked non-doc code”) must report `ddflow lesson add` as unknown, so the expected findings are incomplete. The test (and therefore the implementation it describes) evidently only validates the first token after `ddflow`, silently accepting any trailing words once the first subcommand exists. This makes the core failing-first fixture miss a real drift.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_docscheck_core.py:test_old_readme_yields_exactly_the_three_drifts

chunk_findings.detail: The test asserts that `` `example.com` `` produces no identifier finding while `` `x.gone` `` does. Per the change’s stated intent (“inline-code identifiers … that name nothing in tracked non-doc code”), `example.com` is an inline-code identifier that names nothing in the tree, so it should be reported. The check silently ignores dotted names whose left component is not a tracked file/module, producing a false negative for typos such as `mymod.func` when `mymod` is not a tracked module. The test enshrines that incorrect behaviour.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_docscheck_core.py:test_ignore_names_and_dotted_names

chunk_findings.detail: The test asserts `time.perf_counter() - start < 2.0` while parsing the repository’s live README. On a slow or loaded CI worker (cold cache, disk contention, or a larger README than the pinned commit used by the other fixtures) this check can exceed 2 seconds, failing the test. The assertion is environment-sensitive and not tied to the checker’s correctness.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_docscheck_core.py:test_runtime_on_this_repositorys_readme

chunk_findings.detail: The doc-side flag pattern and the corpus-side flag pattern disagree on one-length flags. `_FLAG = r"--[a-z][a-z0-9]*(?:-[a-z0-9]+)*"` matches a flag whose only character after the dashes is a letter (e.g. `--x`, `--n`), so `_span` calls `_flag("--x", n)`. But `_CORPUS_FLAG = r"(?<![\w-])--[a-z][a-z0-9-]*[a-z0-9]"` requires *two* characters after the dashes (the `[a-z]` plus a trailing `[a-z0-9]`), so the string `--x` can never be captured from any tracked file. Concrete failure: a document contains `` `--x` `` and `cli.py` contains `parser.add_argument("--x")`; the corpus can never contain `--x`, so `_flag` unconditionally appends `Finding("flag", ..., "no tracked code spells this flag")`. Every single-letter long flag is a permanent false positive.
chunk_findings.title: `docscheck.py: _CORPUS_FLAG` (used by `_Corpus.build`, consumed by `_flag`)

chunk_findings.detail: The set of files treated as "code" for the corpus is derived from `doc_globs` via `is_doc`, not from the `docs` argument that is actually scanned: `corpus = _Corpus.build(root, [p for p in files if not is_doc(p) and not p.startswith(".ddflow/")])`. When a caller passes `docs=[...]` with a path that does not match `doc_globs`, that document is both scanned *and* fed into `_Corpus.build`, so the checker validates the document against itself. Concrete failure: `check_docs(repo, docs=["design.rst"])` with default `doc_globs` that only match `*.md` causes `design.rst` to be read as a code file; an inline identifier `` `WidgetFactory` `` that appears nowhere in real code is now in `corpus.words` (and, because the raw file text is scanned, flags spelled only in the document's own fenced examples are in `corpus.flags`), so no finding is produced and the report is (wrongly) clean.
chunk_findings.title: `docscheck.py: check_docs` (corpus construction)

chunk_findings.detail:
`_NOT_PARAGRAPH` does not recognize a bare thematic break such as `***` or `___` (its first alternative requires a space after `-`/`*`/`+`), so such a line is appended to the running setext paragraph. With the input

```
Some text
***
Heading
-------
```

CommonMark renders `Some text`, then a thematic break, then the setext heading `Heading`, so GitHub offers the anchor `heading`. This code instead builds the single paragraph `"Some text *** Heading"` and adds the slug `some-text--heading`, while `heading` is absent from the returned set. A link `[x](#heading)` in the same document (or `other.md#heading` from elsewhere) is therefore reported as `no heading #heading`, a false positive.
chunk_findings.title: `docscheck.py: anchors_of` (paragraph accumulation vs. thematic breaks)

chunk_findings.detail:
`anchors_of` numbers repeated headings by counting occurrences of the *base* slug only:

```python
def add(heading: str) -> None:
    slug = slugify(heading)
    n = seen[slug]
    seen[slug] += 1
    out.add(slug if n == 0 else f"{slug}-{n}")
```

This matches GitHub for plain repeats (`foo`, `foo-1`, `foo-2`), but it does not account for a heading whose natural slug collides with a suffix the tool just generated. `github-slugger` instead loops `while` the candidate is already taken, bumping the suffix, so the anchors diverge and the checker emits a spurious `anchor` finding for a link that is valid on GitHub.

Concrete input — a document `a.md`:

```
# Foo

# Foo

# Foo 1

See [x](#foo-1-1).
```

- GitHub: the three headings get anchors `foo`, `foo-1`, and (because `foo-1` is already taken) `foo-1-1`.
- This code: `add("Foo")` → `foo`; `add("Foo")` → `foo-1`; `add("Foo 1")` computes `slug="foo-1"`, sees `seen["foo-1"]==0`, and does `out.add("foo-1")`, a no-op. `offered` is only `{foo, foo-1}`.

Then in `_link`, `frag="foo-1-1"` is `not in offered`, so the document reports

```
Finding("anchor", "a.md", n, "#foo-1-1", "no heading #foo-1-1 in a.md")
```

for a link that resolves fine on GitHub. The same divergence occurs in the reverse order (e.g. headings `Foo-1`, `Foo`, `Foo` produce `foo-1-1` on GitHub but only `{foo, foo-1}` here). This is a correctness gap in the claimed "GitHub's slug rules" behavior that surfaces as a false-positive finding.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck.py:anchors_of (the inner `add`)

chunk_findings.detail: `_EXT` enumerates the only extensions that make a bare token "path-like", and `_DOTTED_NOT_NAMES` is built from the same list plus a few TLDs. Every other bare filename is routed into `_DOTTED` → `_ident`, and `_ident` emits a finding whenever *any* dot-component is missing from the corpus (`missing = [p for p in parts if p not in self.corpus.words]`, then `if missing:`), so it is reported in the hard-finding kind `"identifier"` rather than demoted to a `"path"` note. Given a doc line such as "the runner writes `results.parquet`" (or `installer.exe`, `logo.jpg`, `notes.ipynb`, `bundle.zip`, `main.ps1`) where no tracked non-doc file contains those words, the result is `Finding("identifier", <doc>, <line>, "results.parquet", "named in no tracked code or path")`; the identical reference written with a slash (`out/results.parquet`) matches `_PATHY`'s second alternative and is only a note. The same token only escapes because a tracked path containing it happens to feed `_Corpus.words` with `"parquet"`/`"results"` — and even then `_ident` still fires if just one component is absent. This contradicts the module's own contract, stated in its header, that path-like inline code naming nothing in the tree is a note ("runtime paths, generated files and illustrative paths -- so a note carries an ignore list instead of failing anyone"): a generated/build-artifact reference in a doc fails the check instead of being reported as a note, and the fix belongs either in `_EXT`/`_DOTTED_NOT_NAMES` or in the ordering so that a token whose last component looks like an extension reaches `_path`.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_FENCE` only accepts a fence whose *absolute* indentation is 0–3 spaces (`^\s{0,3}(`{3,}|~{3,})`), and nothing anywhere handles indented code blocks (four-space) either. In CommonMark a fence's indentation is limited relative to its container, and indented code blocks are code too, so content that a reader sees rendered as a code block is marked `in_code=False` by `_lines` and then scanned as prose by `_Scan.run` (links via `_LINK`, inline code via `_SPAN`), which contradicts the module's stated contract that fenced blocks "are examples, not claims". Concrete input, in a doc that the checker reads, e.g. `docs/guide.md`:

```markdown
1. Configure the client:

    ```
    Set `api_base_url` and see [the API](docs/api.md).
    ```

2. Restart.
```

The fence line has 4 leading spaces, so `_FENCE.match` fails and the following lines are yielded as prose. Given a tree in which `api_base_url` appears only in this sample and `docs/api.md` does not exist, the checker reports an `identifier` finding for `api_base_url` and a `link` finding for `docs/docs/api.md` (resolved relative to `docs/`) — two findings for text that Markdown renders as a literal code block, i.e. exactly the "reader following the doc would hit a wall" false positive the fence-skipping rule exists to prevent. The same happens for a plain four-space indented code block (`    [text](missing.md)`), since `_lines` has no branch for indented code at all.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck.py:_FENCE / _lines / _Scan.run

chunk_findings.detail:
This test asserts a wall-clock budget and a live-content count against the real repository:
`assert time.perf_counter() - start < 2.0` and `assert report.checked["identifiers"] > 50`.
`D.check_docs(root, docs=["README.md"])` does not restrict the corpus to the README — the README's inline identifiers are resolved against *all* tracked non-doc code, so the run reads and scans every tracked code file in the repo (the fixture itself describes a 2600+ line README, i.e. a large tree). On a loaded or throttled CI runner (or a debug-instrumented interpreter) that whole-tree scan can exceed 2.0 s, so the assertion fails even though `docscheck` is correct; and because the bound is on wall-clock time rather than on any property of the output, the failure is non-deterministic and machine-dependent. The companion `checked["identifiers"] > 50` couples the test to the current README text, which this very change set is rewriting ("the day before its catch-up"), so a README edit that lowers the inline-identifier count also fails the test without anything being wrong with the check.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_docscheck_core.py:test_runtime_on_this_repositorys_readme
